text_fidelity_a:
Zinwell ZAT-970A Digital to Analog TV Converter Box (for Antenna Use) We needed to save some money, and I'd heard that Over The Air broadcasts included channels you wouldn't otherwise get. My Dish TV account provided local channels and a whole bunch of channels I didn't use; but the OTA feature really helps!

I paired the Zinwell digital / analog converter box (highly rated, outstanding Amazon price) with the Radio Shack Antennacraft® HDX1000 Amplified HDTV Antenna (also highly rated). You should know one thing -- the mast size for the Dish TV is larger than the mast size for the Antennacraft antenna, so you can't just remove the Dish and replace it with the Antennacraft on the same mast. But it is an easy install.

As a trial, before going up to the roof (2 story house), I set the Antennacraft in the downstairs window that has a view to the southwest (the direction our local TV stations broadcast from). Without the Zinwell, you're limited to the low power analog stations (mostly Spanish language, a few home shopping stations). I think I got about 6 stations. Then I plugged in the Zinwell in line between the antenna and the TV (after disconnecting the Dish TV feed), did a scan, and had 20 channels. Repeated the process upstairs (remember, we have a 2 story) and had 22 channels!! All the local tv stations (NBC, ABC, CW, ION, PBS, etc.) that broadcast digitally came through great!! Unfortunately, it started raining :( so after the rain stopped, I only got as far as getting the mast installed outdoors before it got too dark. It won't take long to finish.

Only one Zinwell related item: You're supposed to be able to choose the feed from the Zinwell to the TV to be either Coax or the Composite (yellow video, red and white audio). I couldn't get the composite to work in setup, but the coax worked just fine. Haven't had a chance to see if, once programmed, the composite would work, or if for some reason I hooked it up to my tv incorrectly (hard to imagine), but ... since the coax works so well, and video and audio quality are great, I'm money ahead and not complaining!!

So when do I break even? $80 antenna plus 2 $40 boxes = $160; Dish TV was costing me about $55/month (yeah, once you've been a subscriber for a while, there's essentially no customer retention policy, so, good by Dish!! -- and that's probably true for Directv and Comcast, too). So after 3 months, essentially at the start of January, I'm home free!! Thanks, Amazon, you're helping me save money, and that's really great!!

NOTE: I only ordered one Zinwell to test out things, now I've ordered a second for our other TV (didn't want to put too much at risk if it didn't work, but it works great!).

NOTE 2: The gov't coupon program is long dead, no hope of getting $40 off on one, just be glad if you waited that these things are as reasonably priced as they are.
text_fidelity_b: Zinwell ZAT-970A Digital to Analog TV Converter Box (for Antenna Use)

VideoSecu Low Profile TV Wall Mount Bracket for Most 32" - 75" LCD LED UHD Plasma HDTV, Compatible with Sony Bravia Samsung LG Haier Vizio Sharp AQUOS Westinghouse Pioneer ProScan Toshiba 1NN The bracket is incredible! I used it on a Samsung Plasma 60 inch ,(600x400-Vesa) PN60F5500. At first I was a little wary. The plasma is 2013 model ,weighs by itself about 60 pounds.Its solid, and the weight of my TV held it down without using security brackets. You need at least an 18 inch long screw driver because you cannot reach behind it once installed. A few turns and you're set. I found it easier to unscrew , first tighten , then go in the opposite direction so it locks the screwdriver in the center making it easier to remove. I left it untighten, since it held in place without them.

Im not a professional installer (like drilling holes and finding a stud in the wall) but was able to use my old screws from the wall to install this mount from my older plasma.. I did however have to drill 2 more at the bottom because of the Vesa difference. Beyond that, everything else was simple.Its solid once installed, very easy, and simple to understand.

CON: Personal pet peeve. The only con is on 60 inch TVs you cannot reach behind easily to use the security brackets.You have to use an 18 inch long screw driver or similar size to tighten them. (booklet does not say this . Only says use a screwdriver)They are not needed because the weight of the TV holds in in place. In my opinion, I like to do everything by the instructions. Not tighten the security brackets made me feel like I skipped a step. I will say its stays in place, and does not move, jiggle etc. Lifting the bottom of a 60 inch is not easy, so there is no worry about it being easily done, even by a kid since the hooks are on the top. Other reviewers have said security brackets are not needed to hold it in place. I just left them barely connected so I could have the option to screw on later.

PS: If you own a 60 inch and im guessing 65 (max size), it will not look like the picture after adding the back portions on the TV. At first I was under the impression it would not work, but adjusted the height on the TV brackets and it fit barely, but did fit.It does work on a (600x400) vesa mount TV.

text_fidelity_a:
Panasonic DMP-BD87 Ultra-Fast Booting Blu-ray Disc Player When we first tried it, the streaming was awful. It couldn't hold a connection to Vudu, to Hulu, or to Netflix.

We ran an update--tricky because it didn't readily hold a solid network connection--and things improved considerably. I can stream Hulu with minor hiccups, Netflix without issues, and Vudu except at 1080p. For the record, I can stream Vudu at 1080p on the TV that the player is connected to. It still supports only a small subset of services, though Hulu has been added. As a streaming media player, it doesn't meet expectations. As a simple blu-ray player, it is quite excellent for the price. It was able to play a few old, slightly scratched DVDs that other players were having trouble loading.

On the signature features, I could find no appreciable difference in boot up or launch time between this and my Sony, or between this with fast boot turned on and this with fast boot turned off. Blu-ray players tend to boot pretty fast in any case. This one allows up to four users to have customized interfaces, but it only affects the background image and color scheme of the interface screen. It does not allow four users to each maintain their own login to Netflix or Hulu, which would be useful if Netflix ever allowed multiple users of an account to maintain their own Watch Instantly queue the way they do with DVD queues.
text_fidelity_b: Panasonic DMP-BD87 Ultra-Fast Booting Blu-ray Disc Player

text_fidelity_a:
iHome Smart Brief: 13 inch Laptop Briefcase for Mac, Heathered Grey This is advertised as a 'sleeve for a 13" laptop' which is such an understatement. Not only will this hold a laptop up to 14 inches, it also has compartments for a cell phone, an IPad or other tablet device (my Kindle fits in there quite nicely) and all the necessary chargers and earphones, making this a one stop transportation and storage device for all personal electronics. There is even a bit of room left over to tuck a newspaper, or a file or two. And, unlike most sleeves, this has handles and an optional shoulder strap.

The compartments are zippered so things should not spill out too easily (although I would open the compartment holding the chargers cautiously). It is a nice, neutral grey color that should not make anyone feel self conscious about carrying it and seems to be reasonably durable. The various compartments seem to be adequately padded against the normal traumas (I don't think I would count on it to protect my computer if it were dropped).

There are a few issues though. First since it is not a typical sleeve it probably would not easily fit into a backpack. Second, fully loaded with a computer, phone, tablet and chargers it will be heavy enough that handling this plus a backpack or briefcase during a commute could be awkward. Third, having everything in one spot could be convenient for travelers except dragging everything out to go through TSA and then repacking it would be time consuming.

Overall this is a great product.

Toploader Zoom 45 Camera Case from Lowepro – Top Loading Case for Your DSLR Camera and Lens I have two camera bags. A huge bag that holds everything camera related and this one. This one is my new favorite. It is small enough to not be awkward, but big enough to carry what you need for a day out on shooting photographs.

It is designed to hold a SLR camera in the vertical position with a telephoto lens. If you are going out shooting with the telephoto, the camera will be ready at your disposal. I like it to carry the telephoto lens as a secondary lens, stored in the bottom of the bag in a horizontal position with the camera and standard lens on top. A sturdy divider separates your telephoto (or any secondary lens for that matter) with the camera on top. A strong nylon shoulder strap allows you to carry the bag anywhere.

The bag also has a nice top zippered closure with extra storage for rolls of film, lens filters, and memory cards or sticks.

Overall this is a wonderfully made and designed camera bag that will at least serve as a good sturdy everyday bag and can even replace larger bulkier bags for your camera transportation and storage needs.

text_fidelity_a:
Jabra Stealth Bluetooth Headset - Black (US Version) I am pleased with this headset; the sound quality is good and audibility is very sharp. The music quality is also good. Assembly is very simple and needs no additional tools to set it together. It also fits well into my ears. I have been using this set for the last three weeks and it works great. It is paired with my cell phone and I use this to listen to the incoming calls and also listen to the music from micro SD card inserted into the cell phone. It is small and has a discreet design. It is very light, easy to carry and works great. The gadget also synchronizes easily with phone, but it does not pair with my Garmin Nuvi GPS machine or my Acer Chromebook both of which are Bluetooth-enabled.

Pairing with cell phone is very easy; just turn the headset on and the cell phone on, it detects the Bluetooth easily and within a minute it gives the message that it is paired. text_fidelity_a:
iHome IHM28W2 Color Changing Alarm Clock FM Radio with USB Charging The home is a decent little alarm clock/speaker, though not always the finest in terms of design.

What does it do?
Acts as an alarm. Some people I noted were annoyed that you had to cycle through the minutes to set the time and alarm and while an hour button is easier, if you hold down the button it really zips through pretty quickly. In other words, you really don't have to plod through minute by minute. To give a sense of that, it took me 10 seconds to speed from 6:00 am to 10:00 am. So really, this isn't much of an issue in my mind. It has two alarms, which is a nice touch. The alarm can go to either the radio or to your input device, though that is a bit iffy depending on your device. It worked with my ipod touch but you're going to want to make sure your device works as it should. One problem is that it is not very easy to see in the dark.

Acts as a radio: the reception was quite good; I had no trouble with local stations. All tuned in well.

Acts as a speaker: the sound is decent for what it is. It certainly isn't going to replace your stereo or even a set of decent bluetooth speakers, but that isn't really its goal and for what it's meant to do, and what its probably target audience is (children, tweens, young teen) I'm sure it's fine.

Work with audio devices--this is a bit mixed. I've had variability with a range of Apple products. They all work in terms of producing sound, but the volume varied amongst them at times so that even with the volume all the way up on both devices it was surprisingly low. Not inaudible or anything, but not loud enough for good entertainment (probably OK for an alarm). You also just basically sit your device atop between two plastic "walls"--there's no cradle or anything and so there isn't much difference between that and just lying it flat next to or atop it. It charged my devices, but it's not a charging cradle, which would have been nicer. Instead there is a USB charge slot on the bottom of the device and you use your own charging cable. The same is true for the audio--you use a cable jack into your device (this one is provided) to link the two. It's an adequate design, if not an elegant one.

Glow/change colors: Well, it does do this. My response? Meh. But then, again, I'm really not I'm assuming the target audience. It doesn't do a anything for me, but kids and tweens might find it interesting. At the least, it isn't obnoxious (not too bright, not too fast-changing, etc.)

it's plastic, but it feels pretty hefty and the build seems decent if a little cheap. I certainly didn't have the sense that it would be fragile or break down soon or anything.

in the end, I'd say it's a decent little device for a tween sort. Not sure it's worth 50 dollars, but it's not exorbitant, just maybe a little pricey. If you're just looking for a speaker, I'd say there are bluetooth ones out there that provide better sound for the price. But if you want a speaker/alarm/radio/something to look at now and then, it's a decent purchase.
text_fidelity_b: iHome IHM28W2 Color Changing Alarm Clock FM Radio with USB Charging

text_fidelity_a:
NETGEAR 8-Port Ultra60 PoE Multi-Gigabit Ethernet Plus Switch (MS108EUP) - Managed, with 4 x PoE++ and 4 x PoE+ @ 230W, Desktop or Wall Mount, and Limited Lifetime Protection I received this item through the Amazon Vine program, although the usual green writing may not be shown. The review is specifically for model: GS305EPP.

Port Binding: I noticed that the Netgear chart shows for the "plus" series of switches, that only models with 16 or more ports support port binding. However, through the web interface, I was able to do a single instance of port binding (it looks like it allows you to bind up to four ports, although I can't think of an instance where binding more than two ports on a five port switch would be worthwhile). I learned some quirks about port binding in the process, that using 802.3ad with multiple Linux servers doesn't allow for more than a Gb of data in any one direction anyway. BUT this switch does apparently support balance-rr, because I could get almost 2Gb/s over a 2Gb aggregate link. I think my hard drives in those machines were maxed out at that point. As I understand it, balance-rr has a high error rate because it uses striping and not all machines support it. But it was working quite nicely with my NAS units and this switch (I was expecting the 8 port switch, which would have made that setup more worthwhile because I could fatten the links on all three servers.

Although my current Netgear Pro AP does not have two ports for binding, I did have an AP before that supported it, in which case that feature on this switch may be an excellent option (particularly considering it is PoE). I haven't done the math for myself, but I think that port binding is almost a gimmick on APs because there is so much overhead on WiFi that even if your AP has a throughput in the multi-Gb range, enough of that is overhead created by the AP that you're not actually getting that much data from one computer to another.

Insight and Web Interface: The Insight App shows this switch (and my Netgear APs) as having "limited support" (just shows basic device info and a link to the device's webpage), so they're not really trying to get users of the "plus" line to subscribe to that in perpetuity.

And you don't need the app to use the switch. You don't even need the configuration page, really: I just plugged this into my old 24-port unmanaged Netgear workhose and it picked up an IP from the router and worked just like an unmanaged switch until I decided to give it a static IP and manage it.

I was really surprised how many features are packed into the management software, considering these are Netgear's lower line of managed devices. But most of the stuff you'll see on huge enterprise devices is here as well (well, it's been a while since I've been inside the big enterprise stuff, but all those goodies reach us as consumers before long).

The web interface is just like any other network device - you can reach it from any webpage and it is super GUI - probably just a little more than I really want it to be, but it is very intuitive and you can find everything with a few clicks. I say "super GUI" just because it looks fancier than I need it to. And one thing I find a little irritating is that when you expand one box, it collapses another, so you can't look at everything at once. This doesn't really matter, but I'm old school where I just want substance over style and even style that doesn't sacrifice substance still looks like they're trying too hard.

PoE: Clearly, on this 4+1 port switch, all four of your devices can use a full 30w each, so this is non-blocking in PoE+ as well as throughput. At time of writing, the 8 port with the same power budget was actually cheaper, so you might consider that, even if you can't use all the ports at full PoE.

What is great about this, is that besides just being able to add APs and IP cameras to your network (or even lighting, etc.), you can turn them on and off from the web interface. So I can keep my main AP on PoE (and therefore on my telecom closet's backup power supply), and then turn my detached garage's AP on and off from the web interface rather than having to go down to the basement and plug or unplug the PoE injector every time I want to use the garage AP (I just turn it on if I'm going to be working out there and might need to watch some "how-to" videos or control my audio system from the local LAN).

*Netgear, if you're listening, I would love to have a super lightweight (and free) app that works remotely (when not necessarily on LAN) to turn ports on and off for exactly this type of reason.*

Construction: Solid device, very dense and professional looking. Plenty of lights that tell you a lot from a glance. Power supply is external and about as big as the device itself. Would personally love a way to rack mount this AND the power supply (for maximum flexibility) in 1 RU, but of course I realize most people don't want to waste a whole rack unit on 5 ports. But for the space both pieces take up, it's about a mid size unit that could be mounted with "wings". It does have four-way keyhole mounts for wall-mounting.

Background: I have great experience with Netgear for my home (but way better than most homes') network. I'd definitely use all their devices were I doing work for small or medium sized businesses. I like them just a tad less when they start trying to sell you subscriptions (which is what I hate about Brocade and Cisco, along with all the proprietary garbage), but for the most part, Netgear is inexpensive and quite reliable. I've had a 24 port nonblocking unmanaged Gb switch running 24/7 in my dusty basement for over 15 years without a single fault AND they still sell that model. Their APs are the best I've had, and I don't think I've ever had a Netgear item break on me, period. I have had lots of other home/SMB stuff break or otherwise have strange issues, though.

That said, there's a lot of no-name PoE switches on the market right now. I don't need any of those handling my low voltage needs OR my data. And they won't beat this line on the price by too much anyway.

This is an excellent device which adds a lot of versatility to your network.
text_fidelity_b: NETGEAR 8-Port Ultra60 PoE Multi-Gigabit Ethernet Plus Switch (MS108EUP) - Managed, with 4 x PoE++ and 4 x PoE+ @ 230W, Desktop or Wall Mount, and Limited Lifetime Protection

text_fidelity_a:
Damero 2pcs/Set Portable Electronic Accessories Travel Organizer, Black I'll admit it right up front: I am an organizer junkie. I love having all of my things laid out perfectly and well organized in all of the different areas of my house. While I try to minimize as much as possible, if I do need to have a variety of items, and let's face it, electronics accessories and cords seem to multiply like rabbits, I want to keep them in an organized, attractive way so that I can always find what I'm looking for and so that they look nice on my shelves.

This two-piece set is meant to be a travel organizer kit for your electronics, but I'm using it in my office to keep all of the excess cords, cards, plugs, etc. for all of my various peripherals. It's fabulous, because I have one that I keep near my computer and one that I keep in my closet, depending on the frequency of use. If I need to get a cord out, it's right there, yet the cases are subtle enough that I don't feel like I'm looking at something overly functional all the time. It just looks neat, clean, and well-planned.

The quality on these is amazing. They are just stiff enough to hold their shape, yet flexible enough that if something's a little bit taller I can close the zipper over it and it's no big deal. The dividers attached by Velcro and so you can move them around so that it works perfectly around whatever it is you want to store and there. I've changed my mind a few times, and it takes two seconds to move the Velcro to hold everything perfectly in place so that it doesn't shift when you move the case around. I don't travel much, but if I did, I would definitely consider getting a second set for on the go. They are lightly padded and so would be a great way of keeping chargers, batteries, and other essential accessories safe. Honestly, I'm such a geek I would probably even use these for toiletries if traveling, because most toiletry cases seem like a messy jumble to me and I like how organized these are.

Overall, if you are on the fence about these, I would hesitate no longer. They are fabulous. I'm only bummed they don't make them big enough to house all the rest of the loose items around my office!
text_fidelity_b: Damero 2pcs/Set Portable Electronic Accessories Travel Organizer, Black

text_fidelity_a:
Sony Cybershot DSC-S600 6MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Zoom This is a point and shoot, so don't expect it to act like a DSLR or even an ultra zoom, but for what it is, it's a fantastic camera.

It starts up quickly and focuses very, very quickly. An AF assist lamp helps with this. The flash is strong and the image quality is very good. The LCD is smaller than most of the competitors in the upper range of the price bracket, but the screen is sharp and very clear. The AA batteries are great because they're cheap and easy to find. I hate it when I'm on a trip and want to shoot a lot, but have to be tethered to a wall socket to charge a battery. The movie mode is wonderful. TRUE 640x480 resolution at 30fps (only with the Pro Duo card) to the limit of the card. I like to take my movies, edit them with a program and burn them to DVD. 480 lines of resolution is TV quality and it looks GOOD. The only real downside to this camera is its bland styling. Other companies are making hot, slim, metal cameras that look good and are difficult to hold, but this camera's plastic body is sturdy and easy to carry in one hand. It has a pleasant weight to it, even if it's a little too wide to fit in a shirt pocket.

There are several websites dedicated to reviewing digital cameras in depth and they can give you technical numbers to compare with other cameras. Since I'm just a guy that occasionally takes photos, I can only talk about my experiences. I like the photos that this takes, I like the way it holds and functions and I like the clarity and smoothness of the movie mode...you really can't compare Sony camera movies to other companies' movie clips; Sony wins, hands down. Sony knows how to cater to their consumers and this camera won't disappoint!

NVIDIA Shield TV | 4K HDR Streaming Media Player The world's first all-in-one Plex box, the Shield comes w/ an unlockable (free) Plex Server inside --and not just another client/player like all other consoles. For those of us w/ a LOT of media, Plex is the pinnacle of enjoying your own media with the best interface possible (and it's free); whereas KODI is the best way for streaming media from the internet. The Shield recognized my old archives instantly, and also when I plugged in a USB3 SanDisk flash drive for extra space. I've had 3 WDTVs, 2 Nexus Players, and 1 MiBox, and I wasted all of that time and money until I got this. I've KODI Phoenix and Exodus for internet streaming, and Plex for my 200 movies, 25 seasons of TV shows, 75 instructional videos (on guitar, magic, and yoga), 6k songs, and all my family albums and artwork. I have the Plex client (player) for TV, phones/tablets, XBox 360, Chromebooks, and Chromebox.

The Shield has BOTH the Play Store and the NVidia Store on its dashboard. I can play all my games again because this console doesn't stutter and freeze up. I'd missed my Asphalt 8 when the others just couldn't handle the workload anymore. I can get even better games from the NVidia Store that the Play Sore doesn't have. Of course, all previous purchases come right back to the Shield --like the HomeRun HD. Plex has a deal they're making w/ HomeRun HD to possibly turn the shield into also doing DVR.

The gamepad has been totally redesigned and has gone from an Ugly Duckling to being prettier than a pail full of kittens. The hex-grip feels good in the hand for shooting zombies or driving on racetracks. The gamepad is rechargeable (yay!) and even comes w/ it's own charging cable. The once $50-extra remote is now included w/ the console. Like the gamepad, the remote also has a headphone jack for discreet listening and a touchscreen volume control and Mute.

So far, with the wrapping ear piece, this pair seems to stay on my ears much better than the buds that just pop into the ears. They paired easily to my iPhone and connect automatically each time I take them out of the case. The sound is decent or at least decent enough for me. I do not use these for just listening to music or videos, I have better over the ear headphones for that purpose. For me, I just use these for running, working out or maybe while working around the yard. For that purpose, the sound quality is pretty good. The only suggestion I have is remember to take the clear tape off the charging contacts; I did not realize it was there and my earbuds were not charging each time I put them back in the case. On the upside, I did learn that the battery life is excellent on these earbuds. I cannot say how long they actually lasted before I charged them, but I probably went on 5 or 6 runs before the first ear bud died. With the tape off the contacts, they do charge automatically each time they are placed back in their case. A nice feature is that the case can be charged either with a cord or by setting the case on a charging pad. The price was reasonable. I would recommend these wireless earbuds to anyone looking for a set. Since I cannot fully say how long they will last or how durable they are, I will reserve the 5th star until I have owned these for a while.

Updated 12May21: Ok, I really want to like earbuds, but I cannot. As many times as I have tried earbuds, they just always feel like they are coming out of my ears, even w/the ear wraps on these buds. Having to continuously re-seat the ear buds in my ears while running just doesn't make for a comfortable run. So, I went back to a pair of wired BT headphones; which sit in my ears much better.

text_fidelity_a:
MIATONE Outdoor Waterproof Portable Bluetooth Speaker Wireless - Green When I first opened the box, I kind of doubted that this compact bluetooth speaker was worth $50. But, after I got it fully charged (which didn't take long) and connected to my phone (super easy), I opened my graphic equalizer app and then started my favorite Pandora station. I cannot say enough about how surprised and pleased I am about the sound quality! The bass is thumping! The treble is crisp and clear! I have other BT speakers this size and none of them even come close to the quality! This Miatone TWS BT speaker is awesome!

Note: because the sound comes out both sides and both ends, you need to keep the control panel at the top (or the bottom). Otherwise, you lose some of the sound quality. So, propping it up in the right position is essential to getting the best quality sound.

I had to knock off one star on the portability factor for one thing; it's a perfect cylinder with no flat edge to keep it from rolling away. And, placing it on end will muffle part of the bass, as both ends have that wonderful bass speaker in them. I guess you can make sure that you place it either on a perfectly flat surface or if it's on a slope, that the included cord is underneath like a 'wheel chock'. But, overall, that's just a minor oversight. I still have to give this amazing little BOOMBOX five stars, because of the quality of construction and the amazing sound. I have JBL's this size that don't sound as good. Super happy with this purchase. Highly recommend.
text_fidelity_b: MIATONE Outdoor Waterproof Portable Bluetooth Speaker Wireless - Green

ETUCRAY Headphone Jack Adapter for Phone Dongle Aux Audio to 3.5mm Cables Earphone Adaptor Headset Splitter for Music&Charger This is a very easy to use timer with some features that I’ve not come across before. It offers three main modes:

1) Clock – standard digital clock
2) Count up timer – can count up from zero to time events. It counts in whole seconds, so it’s not a true stopwatch.
3) Count down timer - you can set it to count down to zero.

The three modes are set by a sliding switch on the left so it’s very easy to change between the modes. It also has a memory feature so you can store a value and re-use it. For example, I use the count down feature to time tea brews, and have set a value of 3 min into memory. To repeat the countdown all I have to do is press the memory button and it sets itself to 3 min.

The best feature is that you can turn off the beep! There are three notification methods: a standard beep, vibrate or a flashing red LED. That’s a huge plus since I usually carry the timer with me and find the beep to be very annoying. The light or vibrate options are far nicer to use. I would imagine the flashing LED light option would be especially appreciated by the hearing impaired. You set the notification type with a switch on the back.

The overall build quality feels very solid. The numbers are large (about 0.75 inches tall) and easy to read even though the screen is not backlit. There a clip on the back that includes a magnet, so you can position this on a fridge or stove hood. The clip does not detach, but the profile is low enough that it doesn’t cause a problem if you want to carry the timer in your pocket.

It runs on 1 AAA battery (included). The package is easy to open – no clamshell to have to wrestle with.

It’s a well-made timer with some great convenience features built in. Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: ETUCRAY Headphone Jack Adapter for Phone Dongle Aux Audio to 3.5mm Cables Earphone Adaptor Headset Splitter for Music&Charger

text_fidelity_a:
(Old Model) Seagate 2TB NAS HDD SATA 6Gb/s 64MB Cache 3.5-Inch Internal Bare Drive (ST2000VN000) I've been a fan of Seagate for many years, since their drives are generally long-lasting and reliable, yet inexpensive compared to comparable items on the market. Over the years, I've never had a Seagate hard drive that I felt died too quickly or had any kind of unexpected problem.

So when I was given the opportunity to test this huge Seagate drive, I was thrilled. Obviously, it's a bare hard drive, so you'll need to know how to open up your computer and connect the drive. Once I did that, the drive was immediately recognized by Windows and the drivers installed automatically. In order to make the drive show up and start working in Windows 7, I had to right-click on computer, click manage, double-click storage, double-click disk management, partition it, give it a drive letter, and format it.

This drive is built to handle 24 hour a day use as storage device attached to a network. Because I am a home user, I am not using the full capability of this drive, but for my purposes, having a huge hard drive to store my collection of horticultural images in raw format, this drive is faster than my other (non-solid-state) drive and I'm not noticing any noise when the data is being accessed.

Overall, this is a huge amount of storage space for the price and would make a great drive for home user or small business user. While you'll probably want a superfast solid-state drive to run Windows and other primary programs, I use a regular drive like this for storage on my computer so that I don't need to buy a 3 TB solid-state drive (do they even make those?).
text_fidelity_b: (Old Model) Seagate 2TB NAS HDD SATA 6Gb/s 64MB Cache 3.5-Inch Internal Bare Drive (ST2000VN000)

text_fidelity_a:
Acme Made Skinny Sleeve Medium (Stretchshell Neoprene) Sapphire/Grey AM10341 So... based on the product description, one can assume that any laptop that runs about 13"-14" should fit neatly into this sleeve. Well, not so much, really. When it arrives you'll see that the tag clearly states that it is for the Macbook Pro/Air 13. Nothing else. No Inspirons, no Yogas, and really not my Alienware 13. Oh, I can squeeze it into the sleeve if I work at it, and if I take the plastic insert out, but it's a lot like trying to fit into your skinny jeans after a weekend of Netflix and ice cream. You can do it, but it's not going to be pretty. And unfortunately getting my laptop back out of the sleeve was even harder. I checked the seams after two insertions and removals, and while they look fine now, I fear that repeated use might be hard on them.

So does it protect my laptop? Well, yes and no. It's in there pretty tightly, so the protective layer is stretched thin. And the end sticks out. I simply can't get it all the way into the sleeve. There's maybe a quarter to half an inch that protrudes. Now if I was tossing this into a briefcase or backpack, I wouldn't worry, but as it is, it's still vulnerable to being dropped along that edge or to being rained on or spilled on.

So overall what I would tell you is this: If you don't have a Macbook Pro/Air 13, then compare the measurements of your laptop to those of that model. If you're not close, look elsewhere.
text_fidelity_b: Acme Made Skinny Sleeve Medium (Stretchshell Neoprene) Sapphire/Grey AM10341

text_fidelity_a: Logitech K750 Wireless Solar Keyboard for Mac — Solar Recharging, Mac-Friendly Keyboard, 2.4GHz Wireless - Silver I normally don't write many negative reviews especially for products that I didn't by from Amazon.  I bought this at a local store as I needed it asap for work. This is amazing in the initial period. I had no problems with wearing out or spring action- feels very good.  Function keys are ideal and the solar app/ light are great resources for letting you know when it is not getting enough light.  I used this on my 2015 MBP for the last two years, but towards the end of second year, it started to "randomly fail" for a few hours at a time.  I ultimately learned that I had to put it in heavy direct sunlight for about 30 minutes to "jump start" it.  I would put it on the car dash in the northern winter to do this (didn't get too cold or hot).  I then had it stop on a dark day and couldn't jump start it-- I tried everything including putting it under a shop light for a bit.  I finally broke down and contacted Logitech.  Now keep in mind that I registered it when I bought--  they suddenly are claiming it was outside of warranty even though I had registered it.  They are telling me to contact the store, but they have no way to pull it up as the store I bought it at is out of business and I paid cash.  I'm really frustrated as I went back and forth with them for almost two months.  I'm at the point where I am keeping the service ticket open as my way of giving them drama.  I ultimately bought the special rechargeable battery that it takes and replaced it despite warnings even on the battery not to do so.  It works for the most part.  I really wish Logitech would address the issue.  I'm also bummed that now that I am on an MBP 2017 15" that they are not making the unifying receiver in USB-C. Nexus 7 from Google (7-Inch, 16 GB, Black) by ASUS (2013) Tablet I received the Nexus 7 as a gift this year for Christmas, and so far I am quite pleased with it. Having a Galaxy Nexus phone, I felt quite comfortable with navigating and configuring the Nexus 7. It's very convenient to be able to share so many apps between my phone and this tablet. The Nexus 7 seems like it's very well built. It has just enough heft to not feel cheap, and the rubberized backing has a nice grip (though this won't matter to most, since a case will likely be the first accessory anyone buys.) The display is wonderful, and has quite a large viewing angle. For such small speakers, I'd say that the Nexus 7 sounds pretty good. I've only charged the device twice, since 12/24, and it gets used quite a bit.

So far, I've used the Nexus 7 for watching videos online (YouTube, Netflix, HBO Go,) streaming music from Amazon Prime, browsing the web, some light gaming with Final Fantasy Dimensions, chatting and computing (Maxima for Android and Wolfram Alpha) and I would say that it's handled everything I've thrown at it like a champ.

The only other tablet I own is a Kindle Fire HD 8.9", which works quite well for reading my technical PDFs, but seems to lack in the other "tablet" departments. I have used an iPad or two in the past. I would have to say that the Nexus 7 is by far my favorite tablet so far.

I'm currently using an Armorsuit screen protector and a Moko slim case that folds into a stand, and would recommend both accessories. I ordered a blue tooth keyboard. I'm hoping that the Nexus 7 with a keyboard might replace my aging netbook.
text_fidelity_b: Nexus 7 from Google (7-Inch, 16 GB, Black) by ASUS (2013) Tablet

I like trackballs for everyday use, and it’s adequate for casual World of Warcraft playing. Most of the time I just futz around leveling alts or doing 5 mans with friends.

But lately I’ve been wanting a mouse I can customize, with more options to adjust my playstyle. It’s cold in my house in the winter, so I wanted to set up mouseover macros and use more mouse buttons, because my hands are cold sitting on the keyboard. So the G502 Proteus Spectrum seemed like a good mouse to review.

I just had one problem: my computer can’t customize the mouse. Why? I have a Mac Book Air.

Now, I know the G502 says on the box that it supports Windows. There’s no mention of Mac support. But I’ve never had a problem with my Mac recognizing Logitech mice, so I figured I’d be safe. What I didn’t know is that Logitech gaming mice have separate software from the Logitech Control Center for regular Logitech mice.

After some Googling, I found the Logitech Gaming Software, which supports Mac OS X 10.8.x and up. I installed it on a Mavericks machine and a Yosemite machine. Neither computer’s Logitech Gaming Software was able to find the mouse. The G502 Proteus CORE is supported, but not the G502 Proteus SPECTRUM.

So right now, I’m unable to customize any of the extra buttons or RGB lighting or any of the other special features. It’s a really fancy basic mouse. I will continue to check for Proteus Spectrum support in the Mac Logitech Gaming Center, and update this review when I can customize things. I’m going into so much detail on the Mac side of things because I know I’m not the only Mac person who tried to use this mouse. I think there’s a workaround with Bootcamp or using a Windows computer, but I’m unable to try that.

I did use the mouse for a few weeks, to test the comfort. I’m really picky on how mice feel in my hand. I’m female and have smaller hands. I like how this mouse didn’t feel too short, and it wasn’t too heavy or wide for me to use comfortably for hours at a time. I also liked the included weights, so you can adjust the weight of the mouse. I haven’t had a mouse with an adjustable weight before, and I liked that extra level of customization.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech G502 Proteus Spectrum RGB Tunable Gaming Mouse, 12,000 DPI On-The-Fly DPI Shifting, Personalized Weight and Balance Tuning with (5) 3.6g Weights, 11 Programmable Buttons

text_fidelity_a:
Kodak PlaySport (Zx3) HD Waterproof Pocket Video Camera (Purple) There's a lot to like about the Playsport. For one, it's very easy to use as a point and shoot should be. The picture quality is certainly fine for just about anybody's use, save for those who really like blowing their pictures up large. It's very fast to move between photos and movie--a few thumb moves is all it takes. The same for toggling between the movie quality. Which means if you suddenly want to grab a still photo while videoing or are worried about recording room and want to drop down a notch or two in quality, you can do so without missing a lot of action. The zoom is a 3X, which is serviceable. I'd prefer longer and I'm sure the next version will offer a longer zoom, but as I use this for quick shots of the family and not for event shooting, the 3X is rarely an issue in terms of not being adequate.

Transfer of files is easy and fast (I use a Mac) and all the cables come bundled with it. Yes, you read that right--it ships with all the needed cables.

Because it is so small and slim, and held in that vertical position, it can get a bit shaky and you'll need to pay attention to keeping it steady, more so than larger cameras or ones you hold with two hands horizontally. The sound pickup is fine save that wind noise can be a problem on windy days--it'll wash out a good deal of the speaking sound.

It feels rugged out of the box and the number of times I've dropped it, including just recently while chasing my boy and his friend around the corner of the house and getting my foot caught in the extension cord of the Halloween decorations. I watched the camera skid across several feet of concrete sidewalk but it was none the worse for wear.

It's slimness makes it a great pocket camera--one of those where it's defined as such not because you can cram it into your pocket and walk around like you have a grapefruit in there but where it slips right in and you barely notice it. That's one of the reasons it's become the camera I take most often when I know I won't need a larger zoom or a flash.

I haven't tried the underwater aspect in actual underwater conditions (snorkeling, say), but a few practice photos in the pool shows it takes pretty sharp photos in that environment. But I'll leave the gauging of that aspect to those more well-versed in such a need.

In the end, it's a great little camera and as mentioned, it's quickly become the one I carry along most often when we're just heading out for some family fun. For post-dusk indoor, I take a Canon elph and for events or hiking a Canon IS with a 12x zoom and a tele-converter. But for playing games in the yard, birthday parties, classroom events, etc.--the Kodak has become the go-to camera.

highly recommended
text_fidelity_b: Kodak PlaySport (Zx3) HD Waterproof Pocket Video Camera (Purple)

text_fidelity_a:
EVOO 14.1” Ultra Thin Laptop FHD, 32GB Storage, 4GB Memory, Micro HDMI, Front Camera, Windows 10 Home I honestly can’t think of an intended user for this laptop. It’s so sluggish that if I gave it to a kid, I can’t imagine them having the patience to wait for the *browser* to open. Let alone go to a website.

I’m a semi-patient adult in my 30s and wanted to chuck this laptop against the wall because the initial setup took so long. For an example, I tried to load the system information to find hardware information, and it took SEVEN seconds to open the Start Menu and load System Information.

The processor is an Intel(R) Celeron(R) CPU N3350 @ 1.10GHz. The laptop has 4GBs of RAM.

My three-year-old phone has 4GB of RAM and is snappier than the EVOO laptop. I have a Chromebook (Acer R11) that is also about three years old, and it’s snappier, too.

Windows 10 S is the default on the laptop, which doesn’t allow you to install any programs not from the Microsoft app store. I suppose that’s useful for basic users, but if you want to put another browser on, you have to disable S mode. Once you disable S mode, you can’t go back to it.

I thought I’d use this laptop for writing, since it’s so slow to load anything that I wouldn’t be tempted to go online. But I don’t even like typing on it; the keyboard feels like I’m typing on a cardboard box. There’s a hollow plastic sound when I type; it’s *that* flimsy. There are some keyboard shortcuts, but I thought it was odd that there wasn’t a shortcut to adjust the brightness. Considering how long it takes the Start Menu to load, that doesn’t make it easy to change the brightness of the screen.

The trackpad is decent, probably the best part of the laptop for me. It has a slightly sandy texture. For an inexpensive laptop, the trackpad isn’t bad.

The laptop is made in China.
text_fidelity_b: EVOO 14.1” Ultra Thin Laptop FHD, 32GB Storage, 4GB Memory, Micro HDMI, Front Camera, Windows 10 Home

text_fidelity_a:
Panasonic DMC-TS6A LUMIX WiFi Enabled Tough Adventure Camera (Blue) I’m a big fan of the Panasonic Lumix line of point and shoot cameras. I’ve been using one for years and, while it has limited features by today’s standards, it has yet to let me down. This latest one in the Lumix line offers a huge range of capabilities, provides outstanding image quality, but continues to suffer from a less than ideal user interface.

The camera comes with just the basics: the camera, a single battery, lanyard and a charger (plus manuals and software). I was a little disappointed right off the bat when I saw the charger. Unlike the older Lumix chargers that had a wall plug built into the charger than flipped out, this has a separate power cord. While that does make it easier to plug into the wall, it also means I have to remember to carry the cord with me to charge it.

Initial setup is straightforward, with the usual time/date setting. Since this has a GPS there’s also the need to go through initializing that option as well. All of these steps can be skipped, but you’ll be reminded to do so every time you power on the camera. It also displays a warning on screen about the waterproof limitations of the camera (and provides ample documentation as to what it can/can’t do re: underwater use).

The view screen is wonderful. Sharp, clear, and easy to read in all lightning conditions. The menu system will be familiar if you’ve ever used a Lumix camera but, if not, it’s still pretty straightforward. I still think Canon has the lead when it comes to having an intuitive point and shoot menu system, but Panasonic does a decent job. I like that with most options there’s a scrolling line of text that comes up to explain what the option is/does. That’s very helpful for options you don’t often use and need help with, but it does not interfere or slow down operation should you know exactly what you want to select.

I won’t list all the camera specs in this review since those are easily available in the listing and the Panasonic web site. Suffice it to say this offers a huge range of options and capabilities that cover pretty much any shooting situation. The Intelligent mode shooting scenario options (of which there are many) are helpful when you just want to point the camera and have it do everything else for you, including compensation for specialized lighting/scene situations. I especially like the macro option, which produced some impressive close-up shots that were sharply focused and clear even though I didn’t use a table-top tripod for stability but relied on the image stabilization features of the camera.

The video recording image quality is excellent good for a point and shoot cam. The performance of the built in mic is decent as well. This won’t compete with a dedicated HD cam, but for casual video shooting it’s a small, simple and easy to use setup that gets the job done pretty well.

The WiFi setup was surprisingly easy. I was dreading that since it often can be a bear, but this was quick and easy, and the included instructions were easy to follow. I use the WiFi option a lot since the USB port to connect to a PC is inside the camera (located under the battery compartment door). It’s done that way to maintain a water-tight shell, but is also means it can be hard to get to easily.

What has not been improved, and actually has slipped a bit, is the overall user interface (e.g., the buttons on the back). They continue to be small, hard to read, and don’t provide solid feedback that they have been pressed. Given that the camera is designed to be used in “rugged” conditions, larger buttons would have been a big plus, especially for zoom and the main menu keypad since those are used so often. Using the menu buttons is hard enough with bare hands; it’s impossible if you have gloves on.

I would certainly recommend this camera if you’re looking for a rugged point and shoot for outdoor use, but also if you’re looking for a high feature camera that never leaves the house. The performance and feature set are both excellent. The user interface brings my rating to four stars but performance and option-wise, this camera offers a lot for the price point.
text_fidelity_b: Panasonic DMC-TS6A LUMIX WiFi Enabled Tough Adventure Camera (Blue)

text_fidelity_a:
Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White Black Friday sales have brought the Echo Dot to under $30, and that is how I am now buying my second one.

So yes, often times you do need to formulate your requests in a certain way (for instance, try asking Alexa how much time it will take to go to work... I gave up on this...) and enunciate them more clearly if you missed, but in general, this technology is just amazing.
Sometimes I even ask Alexa for information I don't need, just for fun.

I like that they named it Alexa. That's so much better than "Okay Google." It feels like a real person. Who in hell at Google thought it's a good idea to force users to use their company name, and thus remind them that their huge creepy analytics private data gathering network is behind it?

Possible improvements:
* Bring back the matte finish from 1st gen. I shouldn't have to pay more to not have it shiny...
* Listen to the word "stop" when the alarm is ringing. Currently you need to wait until it's not ringing and then say "Alexa, stop."
* Add confirmation and modification prompts to "Add a new event to the calendar." Currently if she misunderstood one word, you have to start all over again.
* Alexa bluntly tells you that she cannot tell you about the events in your calendar on a specific date... C'mon guys...
* Implement the word "Repeat": sometimes you didn't hear or didn't catch the information you were looking for, and currently you have to formulate your request again
* Only gives info about the last Amazon order. She can retrieve more order but you have to be very specific about what they contain.
* I wish Alexa could Google more stuff.
* Choose your own wake up word

I never use Siri on my iPhone, but for some reason it feels very natural to use Alexa, maybe because the device is more "fixed" whereas my phone could be in a backpack, in the other room...

The Killer App is MUSIC. We have an Echo Dot in the bedroom, and my wife just loves to ask Alexa for tunes. We have it linked to Spotify.

Also, I am a software engineer, and I have added some custom features through my own skills. I wish somebody came up with something simple to add your own skills, because this is really useful. For instance, the bus comes in front of my house at the most random times, so I developed a skill that tells me in how many minutes the next buses will come. So much faster than having to check a website on my phone!
text_fidelity_b: Echo Dot (2nd Generation) - Smart speaker with Alexa - White

Sound Storm Labs SMC90BB Sound System Weatherproof Bluetooth Amplifier 3 Inch Speakers Inline Volume Control Ideal for Motorcycles ATV and 12 Volt Applications My husband put this on one of the farm Polaris CUV's since installation is beyond what I would able to do. He was able to install it on a ranger using the roof system as the mounting position for the speakers. It installed easily enough - basically clamp the speaker to the roof support bars, make sure to use the included rubber strips to get these to clamp securely or you will be remounting these with the rubber strips again once they slide down. Wiring was simple as it all goes to one plug that attaches to the amp. This does mean you will be mounting all 4 speakers. And since the wiring is together in a harness, some thought is required as to where you put the speakers and a good route to where you want the amp installed. The amp install is simple as it basically needs power (12vdc) and not a lot else. It does come with a handy audio input jack so you can use something like an old iPod for audio input. It also has BNC inputs if you have say a radio that you would want to connect to it so there is some flexibility there. The Bluetooth hook up was simple and works well, but again do not hide the amp behind a lot of metal or this may not work to well.

As far as fit and finish, the only thing I can knock this on is the quality of the clamping hardware finish, but being on a rough duty vehicle this is actually okay.

The bottom line is: Overall installation is simple, and the unit is easy to use.
text_fidelity_b: Sound Storm Labs SMC90BB Sound System Weatherproof Bluetooth Amplifier 3 Inch Speakers Inline Volume Control Ideal for Motorcycles ATV and 12 Volt Applications

text_fidelity_a:
AGPtEK 16GB Portable MP3 Player(Expandable Up to 128GB), Music Player/Voice Recorder/FM Radio with HD Headphone and Adjustable Sport Armband, M28, Black Software Features:
This AGPtEK mp3 player is a really good alternative to an ipod or zune which is more expensive and offers less storage space while offering the opportunity to drag and drop files into the mp3 player folder directly, once it's connected via usb cable to your computer. This feature is important to me, because not all my music is properly tagged, so music organizing software like itunes doesn't recognise the files. This is no problem with the AGPtEK mp3 player, since I can always manually find the file and drop it in.
Hardware Features: The build is attractive and sturdy. I appreciate the glass display and nice solid but light aluminum casing. The shape is a basic rectangle which works fine for me since I like a minimalist look. One thing I don't like about the build is that the click wheel click very loudly and is a little stiff, which is a hassle to use when you're trying to scroll down your music list.The wheel feels a little cheap, its quality is not on par with the rest of the build. The screen is not as large as a typical ipod's but is sufficient. The title of your song will have to scroll a bit to be read fully, which can be kind annoying. ANother great thing is that you can upgrade storage using a micro SD chip which means you're quadrupling your storage. score!

Music Playback features: They have a nice EQ option if you're into that. The fast forward is really slow. The mp3 player plays a bunch of different formats like mp3, oog, wav, flac, etc... You can also store audiobooks, videos, photos, and record sound. I havn't use these features yet.

Accessories: The arm band is a nice bonus. It fits perfectly and leaves holes for charging and headphones. It holds the mp3 player snuggly. The band is smooth and not scratchy. If you have small arms the band can be pretty big, it's adjustable but there will be somg extra band hanging around. t is fastened by velcro.
The headphones are like $10 quality. They're not bad, but they're not audiophile. They don't fit very well as I have small ears but they'll do in a pinch.

Charging: There is an option to charge and transfer or charge and play music once you connect the player to your computer. CHarging it fully takes about 1-2 hours. The mp3's battery is very good, I haven't been able to drain the battery completely, but keeping it off, it's been able to stay charged for over 3 days.

text_fidelity_a:
Aokeo USB Microphone, Condenser Podcast Microphone for Computer. Suitable for Recording, Gaming, Desktop, Windows, Mac, YouTube, Streaming, Discord For the price this is a very nice USB microphone, I would agree with other reviewers that it performs on par with or better than similar competing USB condenser mics in this price range such as Blue Snowball or the Behringer C1.

I do wish it came with more accessories though similar to the non-USB version. The Aokeo AK-60 XLR version comes with a scissor boom arm, shock mount and pop filter for the same price.. so if you do happen to have a compatible audio interface with phantom power then I would recommend the XLR version.

The main annoyance with this mic is that when using it in windows 10 the driver does not have native mic gain control option. In many recording programs you can boost the mic gain via other means but if using this mic for gaming or other purposes through the native drivers then you will have to be very close to the mic to produce adequate volume (ie you pretty much need a boom arm) or otherwise you will need to boost gain via external passthrough program such as APO equalizer. I have also tried this mic in linux and the drivers there do have native gain control.

Overall I do think the sound quality and construction of the mic is good for the price and I would recommend it .. just note that if using windows 10 you will probably either need a boom arm or need to use external software to boost the mic gain. A boom arm is strongly recommended anyways to prevent extraneous noises like keyboard clacking, etc..
text_fidelity_b: Aokeo USB Microphone, Condenser Podcast Microphone for Computer. Suitable for Recording, Gaming, Desktop, Windows, Mac, YouTube, Streaming, Discord

text_fidelity_a:
Acer Aspire One Cloudbook, 11-Inch HD, 32GB, Windows 10, Gray (AO1-131-C9PM) includes Office 365 Personal – 1 year **Discontinued by Manufacturer** There's a lot of reviews already about this product. I wavered for a good while about deciding if I wanted to accept this Cloudbook for review and now kind of wish I hadn't. As far as I'm concerned, the Cloudbook is like a merging of a laptop and a chromebook with neither giving the features that are special to each one. As far as it being a computer, it runs on Windows 10 of which I have great suspicions and doubts. If you remember, I believe most everyone received an offer for a free download of Windows 10 as an upgrade from whatever Windows program they were currently using. I have read from several sources that it was offered only as a way of installing NSA spyware on your computer. We are being watched and monitored at every turn. If you don't believe me, next time you are driving take a look at all the cameras on poles along the roads and highways and tell me we aren't being surveilled. Smartphones, smart TV's, smart refrigerators, dryers and washing machines are simply ways of letting TPTB know what we are doing at all times. How many loads of clothes you washed, what you are doing in your bedroom and on and on. So, what does all this have to do with this little and cute computer? It has Windows 10 installed.

If you are o.k. with that then overall it's not a bad machine. I really miss having a disk drive to load my own personal programs and don't like having to download stuff from the internet via the app store or some other internet source. And since it is a computer but has very little space for storage, you have to have an anti-virus program. It comes with one but it's only good for 30 days and you have to purchase it or get another one. Most of your stuff will be stored in the Cloud (like a chromebook) unless you opt for a Sandisk or external hard drive. And if you buy an external hard drive for more storage why not get a regular computer instead that has more bells and whistles and possibly a disk drive?

It looks like a chromebook and I have had to put a label on it to distinguish it from mine and my kids chromebooks. I'm having a hard time getting used to Windows 10 and it takes a long time to finally get on the internet. I have taped a piece of paper over the camera lens staring me in the face - call me paranoid if you wish but I don't like people in my house uninvited. The "shift" key is way too small and I'm always missing it.

As far as specs go they're listed on the main page but here they are again for your convenience:

11.6" HD Widescreen ComfyView LED-backlit Display (1366 x 768 resolution, 16:9 aspect ratio).
Intel Celeron N3050 Dual-Core Processor 1.6GHz with Intel Burst Technology up to 2.16GHz.
Windows 10
Intel HD Graphics
2GB of DDR3L Onboard Memory.
32GB Internal Storage
Secure Digital (SD) card reader.
802.11ac WiFi (Dual-Band 2.4GHz and 5GHz).
Bluetooth 4.0
Webcam (640 x 480)
High-definition audio support.
Two Built-in Stereo Speakers.
1 - USB 3.0 port
1 - USB 2.0 port
1 - HDMI Port with HDCP support.
Microsoft Office 365 Personal 1-Year Subscription (activation code included).
2-cell Li-polymer battery pack (4200mAh).
Up to 8 hours of battery life (Video Playback).
2.54 lbs. | 1.15kg (system unit only).

If you are already using Windows 10 then it should be easy to navigate, but I feel as if I'm learning a whole new OS though I use Windows 8 on my other laptop. It only detected two of my Bluetooth devices and I have several. If you want Word processing you must redeem your card number inside the box before a certain date or else it expires. And it's all cloud based so your data is out there and not in your pc safe and sound.

I will modify this review as needed, but I have not used this computer since a few days ago and probably will not be using it much at all. I like my chromebook better for web surfing, and it doesn't require an anti-virus program because it's totally cloud based but I never use the cloud. I store the stuff I want on my old desktop or other laptop. And my chromebook has access to a word processing program without having to buy it.
text_fidelity_b: Acer Aspire One Cloudbook, 11-Inch HD, 32GB, Windows 10, Gray (AO1-131-C9PM) includes Office 365 Personal – 1 year **Discontinued by Manufacturer**

MEE audio M6 X1 Wired In-Ear Sports Headphones with Microphone and Remote – Sweatproof Secure Fit Earphones for Running, Jogging, and Gym Workouts (Black) (EP-X1-GYBK) Even pre break-in, these sounded great: probably the best headphones under $20 I've found. After break-in, these MEE buds were sounding like something that cost 4-5 times as much with a nice, even frequency response that favors bass only slightly. I find them comparable to $60-$80 Sennheisers, my previous favorites (which superseded Sony and Koss buds that I also liked). These MEE buds came with 3 sets (S, M, and L) of your typical soft rubber earpieces as well as 2 sets of the interesting multi-tiered earpieces shown in the photos and a pretty standard cloth case. Between the various earpiece options, it's unlikely anyone will have an issue finding a good fit.

The cord is about 1 m long, which suits my purposes. I like the over-the-ear wire bits, too, as they prevent tugs on the cord from dislodging them. They might be awkward with some kinds of glasses, but my straight-earpiece sunglasses fit over them fine. They can be bent to hang down more like normal earbuds if desired, though.

I'll be checking out more MEE products now, seeing what a great value these were. I still favor AKG and Beyerdynamic at the high end, but for my biking/hiking/running/workout listening needs, I'll probably be coming back to MEE.
text_fidelity_b: MEE audio M6 X1 Wired In-Ear Sports Headphones with Microphone and Remote – Sweatproof Secure Fit Earphones for Running, Jogging, and Gym Workouts (Black) (EP-X1-GYBK)

text_fidelity_a:
LeadsaiL Wireless Computer Mouse, 2.4G Portable Slim Cordless Mouse Less Noise for Laptop Optical Mouse with 4 Buttons, AA Battery Used, USB Mouse for Laptop, Desktop, MacBook Great shape, very much like the classic and ubiquitous Logitech. I like that the pairing device is on-board. Lightweight and simple, a mouse is important for me if needing to get serious work done, especially anything with CAD or Visio.

The big question you need to ask yourself is, do you want a Bluetooth version or one like this that has its own receiver. It seems to me that if you always use this with the same computer and you have Bluetooth built in to the computer, then you probably want Bluetooth. Conversely, if you want this to use with multiple computers and/or you don't have Bluetooth built in to any one of the computers you will use the mouse with, then you'd want something like this. This is because pairing is easier in a case such as this, and drivers usually aren't an issue. Bluetooth usually isn't an issue either, but it might get irritating with frequent changing of machines. At least that is my experience.

Does not come with a carry bag, surprisingly. Mouse roller also functions as a button, as it should. It has an on/off switch on the back, which is nice for saving battery life and being able to leave this hooked up to a permanent install (although with a permanent desk setup, I personally stick with wired).
text_fidelity_b: LeadsaiL Wireless Computer Mouse, 2.4G Portable Slim Cordless Mouse Less Noise for Laptop Optical Mouse with 4 Buttons, AA Battery Used, USB Mouse for Laptop, Desktop, MacBook

text_fidelity_a: APC Surge Protector with Telephone, DSL and Coaxial Protection, P11VT3, 3020 Joules, 11 Outlet Surge Protector Power Strip Gray I have been using APC products professionally for years, as part of my job with FEMA. All of our computers, servers, modems, routers and printers are connected through APC UPS units with built in surge protectors, or units like this one,. FEMA goes into areas where storms happen frequently and with great ferocity. Power interruptions and surges are very common. A few months ago, we had an electrical storm in our area, lots of lighting and thunder. We took a pretty good hit somewhere near our house which knocked out power for a pretty large area, and caused some damage to the grid. Unfortunately, the little power strip that I have all my home network gear plugged into didn't stop the surge and it blew out the internal fax modem of my all-in-one printer. (I'm rather disappointed that the house circuit breakers didn't provide enough protection. This is a new home.) Now, we don't fax every day. But, when you need it, you need it and don't want to go to UPS store to fax a simple one page document. We did this for a while. But, finally, I broke down and got a new printer. So, this time, it's going to be well protected. As is everything else in my home network equipment. This APC unit protects ALL of the connections, phone, ethernet, coax AND electrical. It even comes with jumpers for all three data connections. $25 is a small price to pay, to protect over $2,000 worth of equipment. Oh, and just remember that most surge protectors have to be replaced like every three years. This one comes with a LIFETIME warranty with $1000 equipment replacement guarantee. So, good purchase. Five stars.
text_fidelity_b: APC Surge Protector with Telephone, DSL and Coaxial Protection, P11VT3, 3020 Joules, 11 Outlet Surge Protector Power Strip Gray

text_fidelity_a:
Bluetooth Headphones, Anbes Wireless Earbuds, IPX7 Waterproof Sports Earphones with Ear Hooks & Mic, HD Stereo in-Ear Headphones Gym Running Workout, 8 Hours Battery Noise Canceling Headsets When I first got these, I had a problem with the left earpiece not having sound, and the sound that came from the right ear was very tinny. Customer service was absolutely wonderful to resolve this for me very quickly. Since then, the sound is great! I have really small ears and I do find them a bit too big, even with the smallest cover, which keeps me from wearing them as long as I'd like. I haven't actually tried them in wet conditions, so I can't speak to this, but they are very well made and seem like they will last a long time.
--Pros
*Even though I was worried about the earpieces not being switchable, because I am left eared, this has worked alright when I am driving. I just hang the left earpiece on my shirt and use it with my right hand to work the controls.
*Charging is very fast.
*A charge last quite a long time, especially if you only use them for calls. Even listening to music it last a long time.
*The sound is nice and loud with lots of bass for listening to music.
*Call sound quality is great, for me, and for the listening party.
*The are easy to keep up with, using the nice case that they came with. It slips right into my purse or other bag.
*Well made. Durable and made with quality materials.
---Cons
*The earpieces are too large for my ears, even with the smallest cover, and my ears start to hurt after a short time.
*The pieces that go around your ears is shaped in a way that the bottom pushes into the back of my ear, causing it to get very sore.
*They are a bit larger and heavier than I'd like them to be.
*It would be nice to have a small clip for when you are driving, so that you can clip it to your shirt, to be hands free.

Overall, these are great headphones. They need a little tweaking, especially on the earpieces to make them more comfortable on the ears, but I would still highly recommend them.
text_fidelity_b: Bluetooth Headphones, Anbes Wireless Earbuds, IPX7 Waterproof Sports Earphones with Ear Hooks & Mic, HD Stereo in-Ear Headphones Gym Running Workout, 8 Hours Battery Noise Canceling Headsets

text_fidelity_a:
ScreenBeam MyWirelessTV2 Wireless HD Transmitter & Receiver Extender – Wirelessly Connect HDMI-Enabled Media Device to HDTV or Projector Screen, Full HD 1080P, 150 Foot Range POSITIVE:

I had been expecting cheap looking/feeling components because one review mentioned that that was the case, and because I am unfamiliar with the brand. Contrarily, every single element of this package feels of good quality. The main units are well formed and have all the ports, buttons, and LEDs that you could want for the application; every cable you need comes with the package, they are good quality, and they even include hook and loop mounts for the IR receiver and transmitter; the on screen menu is simple but well done, and even translucent over the video you are watching; the rectifiers are the type that can fit on most power strips; the unit uses wireless N technology on ~5GHz; the two devices are pre-paired; and the packaging and included literature even looks good.

Nothing about this unit seems cheap.

NEUTRAL:

I'm guessing the reason that some people cannot get an acceptable signal is because they are experiencing interference with their WiFi network; this can be rectified in some cases.

Common consumer frequency bands are ~2.4GHz and ~5GHz. Most new wireless access points/routers transmit at BOTH frequencies, but usually, either of them can be turned off if you go into your router settings (usually 192.168.0.1 or 192.168.1.1 from a web browser by factory default). A lot of people have all their electronics clumped together near the TV, so this could be especially burdensome in that situation. Many routers automatically change bands within the given range to avoid interference, but I cannot know what exact frequency these run on. Try turning the 5GHz band off on your wireless access point/router or move other 5GHz wireless devices away from these.

I didn't experience any problems turning my two 5GHz wireless access points on and off from different locations around the house. I could get plenty of signal from the basement up to the second floor and over a room with no problem, this even going through a few layers of plaster, which - as a non-porous material - the manual warns you may degrade the signal.

NEGATIVE:

Well, all wireless things are finicky, as are shortcuts to doing things in most cases. This works well, actually, but I did have trouble with both my computer and my DVR:

My computer's HDMI output, like most, tells the computer when something is plugged in, so the computer changes its mode. But since the connected hardware (the transmitting unit) is not using the signal immediately, the computer didn't recognize it. I had to first get the computer used to the setup by plugging it directly into the TV's HDMI port and then quickly switch ports to this unit. But then I had trouble with the audio as well. It took a while, but I eventually got it. The problem is, I suspect you'd have this problem every time, so I do not recommend this for use with a computer. I'm guessing a cell phone's micro-HDMI port would have the same problem.

I also couldn't get this to work with my security system's DVR, and I suspect it's the exact same problem, since the DVR does function like a computer in many ways. However, it is clear to me that this is primarily made for a cable or satellite box.

Again, less finicky than I expected. I am unsure if the correct hardware exists to make the computer recognize this device when plugged in via HDMI.

I hate to leave two things turned on all the time, especially because the radios will always run and consume some power (admittedly little, as both units consume around 5 watts when running, probably less than one when idle).

UNSOLICITED ADVICE:

1. I let the cable company slide when it kept jacking up prices and charging me for sports networks that I never watch. But when they started encrypting their signals to force every TV in every house to have a box attached to it (so they could make it easy for you to buy Pay Per View), I finally had enough and cancelled my cable. Those boxes are so slow and unresponsive, not to mention ugly and make your TV work less well than it should. I installed an antenna system in my attic (actually, in my case, above the 8' mark of my attic, so no usable space was wasted) and now I get around 45 free channels, and all the networks are in HD. Best thing I've ever done. If you own your house and/or will be living where you are for a while, I encourage you to do the same. Check out tvfool dot com to start your research (free). Or just cut the cable anyway because you're tired of being lied to and price gouged.

2. I ran proper in-wall cabling systems for a home network, security system, multiple video systems, and whole house audio system all at the same time. Second best thing I've ever done. You wouldn't believe how often it comes in handy and you'll never need finicky shortcuts again. If you own your house and are decent at DIY, I encourage you to do the same. More is better; run more cables than you need, because running them is the hard part.
text_fidelity_b: ScreenBeam MyWirelessTV2 Wireless HD Transmitter & Receiver Extender – Wirelessly Connect HDMI-Enabled Media Device to HDTV or Projector Screen, Full HD 1080P, 150 Foot Range

Philips DVT5000/00 4 GB Digital Voice Tracer with 3 Built-in Microphones Voice Recorder This is a good voice recorder. Whether you need it to record your voice memos, lectures, meetings, or discretely record your favorite spy, this will surely be a recorder you'll find many uses for.

It feels very secure in your hand, and has a comfortable feel and weight. It comes with a small pouch, which is nice. The record button is easy to find my sight or feel. The volume and forward/reverse buttons are on an outer button from the record button. Play and stop on the left and index and menu are on the right.

f1 and f2 buttons are primarily used for setting mic sensitivity and voice quality. Under Mic Sensitivity you can choose: Dictate (good for personal memos), Speech recognition (turns on when it hears voice), conversation (good for interviews or conversations, auto zoom (good for large areas where there may be close up voices and far voices), and lecture (good for lectures)

You can choose either low quality at 8kbps in Mp3 format to super high quality 192kbps in mp3. There is also a wave format in 1411 kbps. The higher quality you go impacts total record time. You can add a micro SD card for adding recording time.

There are also 4 index folders labeled A thru D. These are for separating projects. There is also a folder you could place music files if you wanted this to be a mp3 player.

There is also a menu setting where the voice quality and mic sensitivity can be accessed as well as numerous other options such as splitting files, display contrast, and clearvoice (an option that improves the sound quality of the recorded voiec)

The unit comes with rechargable AA batteries that will need to be charged when you first open it. They charge with the included usb to micro USB cord. Any other micro USB cord you own will also work. Once the recorder is connected to your computer through the USB cable you can download and upload voice or mp3 and wave files.

The only thing I wish this had was different settings for each index. For instance I would have liked to set index A for lecture mode at high quality, index B for dictate at a lower quality, etc. Once you set a mic sensitivity and recording quality, they are the same for all index until you change them in settings.

Overall a great quality recorder. Great for meetings, memos, and conversations.
text_fidelity_b: Philips DVT5000/00 4 GB Digital Voice Tracer with 3 Built-in Microphones Voice Recorder

Linksys WiFi Extender, WiFi 6 Range Booster, Dual-Band Booster, Internet Repeater, 2,000 Sq. ft Coverage, Speeds up to (AX1800) 1.8Gbps - RE7310 You should know up front that this extender only works wirelessly with dual-band WiFi routers (routers with both 2.4GHz and 5GHz).

But it will work as a hard-wired range extender for single-band routers (2.4GHz) using an ethernet cable.

If you have a single band router like we do, it will not detect the wireless network or connect wirelessly. If our neighborhood is any indication, this extender won't work with most home routers. Out of the ten or so visible wireless networks in our area, the extender only detected one or two. The two it detected were two of the weaker signals, but I assume were dual band signals the extender would work with.

After several frustrating attempts to get it connected wirelessly, I spent about an hour with customer support before being informed of this limitation on the extender. The product listing says "compatible with all Wi-Fi routers," and it may be compatible with all routers if set up as a wired extender, but apparently it isn't compatible with all as a wirelessly connected extender. If you want wireless connection to your router, check your router's capability and make sure it is a dual-band router before ordering.

As I mentioned, I did get it set up as a wire-connected extender using an ethernet cable. And it works well for that. It puts a good strong WiFi signal all over our house and much of the yard. I'm giving it four stars for that.
text_fidelity_b: Linksys WiFi Extender, WiFi 6 Range Booster, Dual-Band Booster, Internet Repeater, 2,000 Sq. ft Coverage, Speeds up to (AX1800) 1.8Gbps - RE7310
