text_fidelity_a:
iHome iAVS16 Bedside Speaker with Alexa Built In, Bluetooth, and USB Charging, Now Supports Spotify by Voice This is a pretty mixed review of an interesting concept that is pretty good right now, but has the potential to be great in the near future. At the current price of about $150, this is ok+ based on the following criteria:

Sound Quality: 2.5-3 stars
For the size, it's ok
When reviewing for sound quality, I compare speakers (and headphones) to comparably sized items, based on speakers I currently or previously have owned. I take price range *somewhat* into account (I don't expect $15 headphones to sound like $500 ones), but for anything over $100, I use the full range from the cheapest stuff I have, to my favorite brand, Bose.
So with that in mind, I have a portable wireless Bose speaker that is smaller and acts as the "5" on the scale.
The sound on this can get loud enough to not distort and still fill a smallish room or normal bedroom fine. The treble and bass are ok, though the higher ranges are tinny and the bass lacks depth. Overall sound from high to low and throughout the mid range lack definition. It's good enough for very casual background listening and for podcasts.

Alexa Feature: 4 stars
I have an iPhone and think Alexa has quite a bit more understanding and skill than Siri. When asked questions, from simple stuff like "what's the weather" to more complicated stuff like "I'm hungry. What can I make in half an hour?", the answers and follow-up questions are highly intuitive and thorough. Does she get everything all the time? No. But she does a much better job than Siri.

User-Friendliness: 2.5 stars
I didn't like the process of figuring out how this works, particularly the part of pairing with more than one device and also Having to use an app to make most of it work. It was a clunky, irritating process that more or less stayed that way every time I wanted to use this thing, especially for listening to music. It should be able to just play from your iTunes through the iTunes app and bluetooth, and instead, I was only able to make it play iTunes though Their App, which sucks when it comes to my music. And that brings us to the App..

App: 2 stars
No. Just no. Bluetooth exists for a reason, and if a speaker has bluetooth, you should be able to just pair and play. I had to use the app to play from my iTunes, and because I have a very specific way of organizing things, I was incredibly annoyed that something didn't translate, and my music was disorganized and basically impossible to search for with this app. Instead of being able to play what I want from one of my playlist subfolders, it disregarded my way of organizing things, and I ended up giving up. If I can't listen to my stuff easily with this, then like 75% of the reason to use this disappears, leaving me with an expensive alarm clock with weather report, recipe ideas, and some cool internet stuff. That's cool, but it's quite incomplete for what I need, and what I suspect many people want.

tl;dr version: sound is mediocre but doable, app is bad, Alexa is super clever and smart, and the experience has a lot of frustrating aspects.
text_fidelity_b: iHome iAVS16 Bedside Speaker with Alexa Built In, Bluetooth, and USB Charging, Now Supports Spotify by Voice

text_fidelity_a:
D-Link Wi-Fi Camera with Remote Viewing (DCS-930L) (Discontinued by Manufacturer) Compared to a similar camera made by Belkin, setting up the D-Link was kind of a pain. Not as much of a pain as setting up a Foscam F18918W - where you get directed to a third party domain name provider and get to learn the joys of port forwarding - but a relative hassle.

For the Belkin, I opened the box, plugged into my router, ran a set up program that took less than five minutes, downloaded an app, and I was up and running. While this is a very similar product in both look and function, it took over an hour - and two ethernet cables - to set it up. There is no Mac software on the installation cd. The box states that a Windows pc is required, but the website has a Mac download available. You have to scroll through the product photos, which aren't in alphanumeric order. Just keep looking until you find the DCS-930L - AFTER the 931L and the 932L and the 934L. Have faith. Keep going. It's there.

Once you get the program installed, it takes very little time to *find* the camera and teach it to log into your wireless network. And then you are back to the website to set up your account and view your camera. Except you are on a Mac, and the viewer requires you to install the Java Runtime Environment. JRE is a big old security vulnerability on Macs. So much so that Apple advises against using it. Mavericks lets you turn it on case by case - and, by default, it will ask you every time before running it. If you are on an OS below Mavericks, check the googles for setting your preferences so that you're not running JRE all the time.

Okay, so now you've got JRE going, and the first thing the program tells you is that you have to update your firmware AND you need to have the camera AND your computer ethernet-jacked right into your router. LOLWUT? I'm lucky. I am on a laptop, and I have an extra ethernet cable and an empty port. So, I did that, and there I was, up and running, about an hour, hour and a half, thereabouts, after I started.

Image quality is pretty good - not great. Audio is okay. The settings are very customizable. But the wifi receiver is very weak, and that limits the usefulness of this product.
text_fidelity_b: D-Link Wi-Fi Camera with Remote Viewing (DCS-930L) (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

SereneLife Battery Grass Cutter, Grass Clippers Cordless, Trimmer Cutter, Handheld Trimmer, Grass Shear Electric, Perfect for Leaves & Debris, Rechargeable Battery, Charge Time 4 Hrs, 3.6V Here are my thoughts about Roku. Generally I like the product, but in setting it up I had some concerns.

PROS:
**Easy to set up
**Compact - it's so small it fits in one hand.
**Picture quality is pretty sharp depending upon the source. It is not HD quality but more like a decent DVD (though not Blu-Ray).
**A number of free channels available through Roku. You can add a lot of content. Since I'm an old movie buff, I added Pub a Hub (public domain movies) and Crackle (pretty bad recent movies but some good classics, like Easy Rider).
**Picture is big. I have a friend who has a projector that's five times as big as the Roku, and yet the projected image is the same size. That's impressive.

CONS:
**How much radiation does this device emit? In the fine print, the instruction booklet reads: "This equipment complies with FCC radiation exposure limits set forth for an uncontrolled environment. This equipment should be installed and operated with minimum distance 20CM between the RADIATOR AND YOUR BODY."
Hmm. I don't know about you, but it's hard not to sit pretty close to the projector. I used it in the bedroom and watched a movie on the ceiling. Of course I had to be close to it in order to put it at the right angle. How much radiation is the device emitting?

**Roku asks for your credit card information before you can use the device. When you set up an account, even if you don't want anything other than the free channels, they force you to put your credit card on file. The other privacy issue I object to is the way Roku allows you to connect to Facebook. In order for Roku to work, you were pretty much forced to allow Roku to access your information on Facebook at any time (even when you're logged out!) Not happy about this.

**In order to add some channels to the Roku network, you have to establish separate accounts. That means establishing one for Netflix, one for Amazon, etc, if you don't already have one. This means I'm sharing my account information with a number of companies I may or may not want to do business with. No doubt all this information will be shared among the video providers. That means a lot of spam will be coming my way in my email.

**Roku is geared toward convincing you to subscribe to as many streaming (pay on demand) services as possible. I'm not sure I would pay $300 for it, as it is very much a device aimed to getting you to subscribe to streaming channels. You can use it other ways, but Roku feels like a product sponsored by many vendors, as opposed to a stand-alone projector.

My conclusion? I recommend it with some reservations as noted above.
text_fidelity_b: SereneLife Battery Grass Cutter, Grass Clippers Cordless, Trimmer Cutter, Handheld Trimmer, Grass Shear Electric, Perfect for Leaves & Debris, Rechargeable Battery, Charge Time 4 Hrs, 3.6V

Fujifilm Finepix F70EXR 10MP Super CCD Digital Camera with 10x Optical Dual Image Stabilized Zoom and 2.7 inch LCD The Fuji F70 EXR has features which clearly depart from the "same old, just a little better" way of doing things. For one, it puts the camera's digital nature front and center and manipulates images to improve them. Starting with the common auto red eye reduction, extending to pixel binning for high dynamic range or low light shots in EXR mode, as well as merging multiple shots in the natural light flash, pro low light and pro focus modes. Couple such digital magic with a great new sensor and a good zoom lens, packaged into a very small, attractive camera, and you have a real winner. In Auto EXR mode it even switches automatically to macro mode when needed, a feature I wanted for the longest time.

My favorite mode is EXR high dynamic range. On a recent trip through the Southwest US I pretty much left the camera in this mode with the Velvia film simulation (i.e. vivid colors), and all outdoor shots turned out great. Stunning, vivid colors, good detail in highlights and shadows, and nothing overdone. Simply cool!

Originally I bought the F70EXR for low light shots at work because the new sensor and software promised to yield better results than older PnSes, and it does. I have sharp handheld shots without flash that I simply have never been able to take with any other point and shoot (or older SLR for that matter). I alternate between EXR high iso/low noise, natural flash and SP night modes for this, depending on the situation or how much time I have to think and plan.

Overall, this camera is fun to use and gives great pictures almost all of the time.

Pros:
small and light
great auto modes, especially high dynamic range EXR
nice 10x zoom lens - love the range
great sensor, larger than average for PnS
smart software
fast focus and time to shoot
high quality bright display

Cons:
pronounced purple fringing (chromatic aberration) around bright, high contrast edges
finicky zoom lever - I wish it had two levels of sensitivity

Quibbles:
mode wheel turns too easily for me
some modes have overlapping features, makes choices confusing (e.g. Astia film simulation for soft tones vs. two portrait modes which promise soft skin tones)
multi shot modes are impossible if subject doesn't hold absolutely still
on/off button somewhat difficult to find by touch for me
would be nice if the lens defaulted to somewhere between 35 and 50 mm equivalent focal length instead of the very wide angle 27 mm
text_fidelity_b: Fujifilm Finepix F70EXR 10MP Super CCD Digital Camera with 10x Optical Dual Image Stabilized Zoom and 2.7 inch LCD

text_fidelity_a:
Mad Catz R.A.T. 7 Albino Edition Professional Gaming Mouse The Rat 7 mouse seems to be going for the customization market, but where it really excels is in simple build quality. The weight, smooth precision parts, and mechanical functioning of this mouse make it feel less like a peripheral and more like a piece of tactical combat gear. The buttons are well placed, the macro customization is deep, it slides smoothly without catching, and the sensor does its job very well.

My gripes are mostly minor. Just about everything on this mouse is movable or can be switched out for alternate parts, even the weight and balance are adjustable, but I found that as much as I wanted to use the grippy parts in some places, they just didn't feel right, while the slick pieces are awesome. There are two small hex bolts that I find to be unfortunately placed. One rests right under your thumb, and the other under whichever finger you hold on the right of the mouse. They aren't uncomfortable, and may even help orient your hand position, but I find they break up the otherwise smooth feel of the mouse. The action on the scroll wheel and button clicks are very nice. My one criticism on the sensor is that the hole is very small and tends to collect small lint particles that can interfere with the sensing.

The only time I find myself hitting buttons on accident is when picking up the mouse, I often hit the forward and back buttons, which can be irritating in web pages, but can always be remapped. There is a really well placed little red button above the thumb that triggers a fine tuned aiming mode. As much as I like the feature, I'd really like to be able to map this button to something else on occasion, but haven't found an option to do so.

Everything you need to do with the mouse, you can access from the mouse. The tools for adjustment are built in, the button for changing between function sets is accessible, but hard to hit on accident, and changes color with mode. Perhaps my favorite feature on the Rat 7 is the small rocker switch behind the scroll wheel which can be used to raise and lower the mouse sensitivity (pointer speed) on the fly, which nearly makes the precision aim button obsolete.

I'm used to using an ambidextrous mouse and switching hands often. This mouse can be used left handed without much difficulty, but you lose access to some of the buttons and features when doing so, most notably the horizontal scroll. Overall a very nice purchase and I'm quite pleased with it. More than worth the price difference between it and the lesser mice on the market.
text_fidelity_b: Mad Catz R.A.T. 7 Albino Edition Professional Gaming Mouse

Seagate Expansion Desktop 12TB External Hard Drive HDD - USB 3.0 for PC Laptop (STEB12000400) The perfect external 3.5" hard drive for purchase at this point in time as far as I'm concerned: they include controller software *if you want it*, but they don't try to persuade you to use it, instead taking the simplistic approach, which is plug it in and use it! I would never use software to run a hard drive anyway.

Also, 4TB seems to be the sweet spot right now for price/size ratio for external 3.5" storage (3.5" drives always require an external power source, whereas 2.5" external drives - which are sometimes slower - usually do not). I like that you can leave it plugged in, but it only powers on when you attach the USB cable.

USB 3.0 really is a vast improvement over previous versions. I'm dumping all my files from five other drives on this monster, and 500GB are transferring through the computer from one drive to another in around 2-3 hours, both large and tiny files.

Worth noting is that the case seems very thin around the drive, which is probably good for heat dispersion, but will not provide the kind of protection you'd want if you were constantly transporting this drive.

I now have on here hundreds of seasons of TV shows, most in HD, nearly a thousand movies, most in HD, hundreds of music albums, books, maps, comics, software setup files, etc., and I STILL have room to grow. To get all these things consolidated and organized - and all accessible with a single drive powered up - is really fantastic.

Samsung BD-H5900 3D Blu-Ray Disc Player (2014 Model) Packaging--very minimal, which is nice. Box was just enough to fit the machine safely and snugly--no over packaging

Apps: Seems to be a lot of back and forth on Amazon Prime. Mine definitely does not support. These are the apps from the newest software update (June 20th, 2014)
hulu plus,
VUDU
Youube
Netflix
Opera TV store
Flixster
CinemaNow
Rhapsody
Picasa
AccuWEather
Twitter
Pandora
Target
Internet TV--horrible interface

To be honest, I wouldn't use most of these, so I'm not all that impressed with the Apps, though certainly they have the most needed on one in Netflix. But as I have Amazon Prime, I'm sticking with our DVD player that allows me to access it (I also have an Apple TV, which is why these apps don't do much for me). Build quality: I don't know if it really matters at all with a DVD player--I mean, it's going to sit up there and not really get any abuse I assume. But it does feel a bit light, not all that solid. If it were something portable and had that feel, I'd have some concerns. Not so much with this kind of device. It has a relatively small footprint.

I had not problem with several DVDs, both blu-ray and regular. Menu movement was fast, start-up time no different from any others I've used--not noticeably better or worse. Picture was fine, again, no better or worse than others I've sued (Sony, JVC)

screen is a bit too bright. Personally, I'd find it annoying, but others may not notice.

It's not a bad player at all, does most of what it needs to OK, but I definitely prefer our Sony for its larger app features and dimmer screen (it also feels more sturdy).

12x56 Monocular Telescope for Smartphone - Monoculars for Adults High Powered High Definition with Phone Adapter Tripod Clear Low Light Night Vision Telescopes for Hiking Hunting Bird Watching Camping The monocular works great, including in low light as advertised. It feels as solid as my name-brand binoculars, not like cheap plastic like some off-brands.

I’ve had binocular clips for phone cameras before this one, but this is the most sturdy design I’ve seen. I love it! I get very sick from shaking which meant for a long time monoculars were out of the question as well as some binoculars. It’s difficult to follow fast moving birds, but for ones that are sitting still this is an excellent option! I have a Pixel 6 Pro and had no problems hooking it up to the monoscope and giving it a whirl.

The tripod included is alright, it’s solid enough and when tightened well it works great, I found it a little fiddly to tighten and accidentally knocked off one of the knobs! It can hold the monoscope and my phone just fine despite the imbalance, and the universal mount means you can always use your tripod of choice.

We took some pictures from the cliffs near where we live, it’s pretty powerful. I also took a photo of the moon, you could see the pits and craters. It can be difficult to aim, especially at night but it seems to take practice–I didn’t use the tripod for that shot, which would have made it clearer. The woodchuck is with a tripod and fully zoomed.

What made me interested was the carrying case, which would fit perfectly into a hiking day-bag. My husband and I love to bird and this would be great for spotting owls at dusk! It’s stronger than my standard binoculars.

I shopped at a variety of stores. I was surprised to find that some of the companies known for sturdy cell phone cases did not offer the same quality to fit tablets. Notably absent was protection for the corners.
My search finally paid off as the ZUGU case is ideal. it is sturdy without excessive bulk. It protects all sides of the tablet including the corners. The cover projects a bit above both the camera lens and the tablet screen to protect them. The stand folds easily on the outside of the case. It is thin but stiff enough to hold the tablet at various angles and the magnetic attachment is a unique feature, securing the device without slippage. (I observed that some cases can flop unpredictably or are very limited in their options for viewing angles.)
Given the snug fit, I found it initially a challenge to attach the ZUGU case. . This is before I found the best approach was to slip the top right hand corner of the case last over the tablet frame. Due to the openings, the case material was s thinner and more flexible here. But do be careful not to pull too hard: The corner should slip readily over the frame here if the remaining sides are snug.
Another unique feature is that the company may offer to cover the copay if the owner has Apple Care and the screen breaks. (Please check the manufacturer website for detail).I
There is one trade.off with the case: it is purely functional rather than being a fashion statement. But I personally prefer protection to good looks and will enclose it with some confidence in a tote.

text_fidelity_a:
Logitech for Creators Blue Yeti X Professional USB Condenser Microphone for PC, Mac,Gaming,Recording, Streaming, Podcasting on PC, Desktop Mic High-Res Metering, LED Lighting,Blue VO!CE Effects-Black This is a fancier version of the popular Blue Yeti amateur-quality USB microphone with a much higher price tag ($170 vs $110). For the extra money, you get 4 condensers (instead of 3) to give you higher-resolution 24-bit audio (instead of 16-bit) plus a bunch of fancier control and display options. The new microphone has the same directional recording patterns to isolate the recording to your intended audio sources. Is the new microphone worth the extra money? If you really need 24-bit audio, then definitely yes. If not, the new display and control features are more convenient than a huge jump in functionality. The Blue Yeti is still a great microphone for amateur USB recording (podcasts, musical performances, etc). The new version is a step forward, but not worth the price for everyone.

My biggest complaint is that the new microphone uses the same ancient mini-USB interface as the old one. Modern ultralight laptops are moving to the USB-C standard and mini-USB is 2 generations old. You could use a USB-C hub to give you a mini-USB interface, but I wish all modern devices came with USB-C ports since this has been the standard for the last few years.
text_fidelity_b: Logitech for Creators Blue Yeti X Professional USB Condenser Microphone for PC, Mac,Gaming,Recording, Streaming, Podcasting on PC, Desktop Mic High-Res Metering, LED Lighting,Blue VO!CE Effects-Black

text_fidelity_a:
Gskyer Telescope 600x90mm AZ Astronomical Refractor Telescope for Kids, Adults Astronomy, German Technology Scope Even though I have always had an interest in astronomy I was never able to work a course in this subject in my college schedule or afterwards. When I saw this telescope offered I realized that now I had both the time and the means to explore my interest a bit further. I had very little difficulty setting the scope up, and spent some time familiarizing myself with the various components. I practiced using this by checking out objects in my neighborhood, and managed to get an 'up close and personal' view of some birds in a neighbor's yard and quickly realized that this scope was powerful.

That evening I took the scope to an upstairs window to see what I could see, and despite the pesky street light was able to get a great view of the full moon (btw did you know that it sparkles a bit?). I saw details that I had only seen in photos before which was fascinating. Then I decided to take a look at Mars, which was near the Moon that evening. That is when things got complicated. The finder scope and the main scope need to be synced, and I don't know how to do this (yet). With some fiddling, and aided by Mars' close proximity to the Moon I was able to find Mars, which was exciting but for some reason it was distorted (it had a starburst appearance). My husband and I fiddled with various lenses and combinations to try to eliminate this but were unsuccessful. The experimentation was further complicated by the touchiness of the stand....it was difficult to make small, smooth adjustments and to keep the scope locked in position. Some of this is no doubt due to our in expertise, some I think is due to the equipment.

My enjoyment of this scope would have been much greater if more instructions had been provided. We discovered, more or less by accident how to lock, at least partially, the scope into place. We managed to make some focusing adjustments by trial and error. Even some rudimentary instructions in a small booklet or even a sheet or two describing how to adjust, focus and lock the scope as well as an illustration of the scope with all the components clearly labeled with a brief description of their function would have been greatly appreciated. This is a basic instrument, one that will primarily be used by beginners or novices who will not necessarily be familiar with this equipment. Basic instructions should have been included. As it is my unfamiliarity with the various aspects of the telescope make following many of the instructions I do find on-line difficult to follow.

Despite this problems I am enjoying my new toy. I found the stand to be steady, and the tray located on the stand to be a handy place to put lenses and covers. As I mentioned earlier this is a surprisingly (at least to this beginning user) powerful scope. I'm going to play around with this some more, and will probably upgrade some of the lenses and add some accessories based on my experiences. Besides star gazing I think this will be a great item to watch birds or wild life, and it is certainly portable and forgiving enough to take on a camping trip.
text_fidelity_b: Gskyer Telescope 600x90mm AZ Astronomical Refractor Telescope for Kids, Adults Astronomy, German Technology Scope

text_fidelity_a:
Bestlight Ultra-Bright LED 36 Camera / Video Light with Rechargeable Battery Pack and Charger for Canon, Nikon, Olympus, Pentax DSLR, Mini-DSLR and Camcorders This is an great value in a light panel. While the size limits the amount of light output (compared with larger models made by Bestlight) the size makes this far more workable on smaller cameras.

I've used a couple of their larger models, and they are fine for hefty DSLRs. But, when put on a smaller camera it makes it so top-heavy that it topples over. This one, however, is so small and light (it is less than 2.5 inches wide and weights only 2.1 ounces including the battery) that it worked fine on my Powershot without making it top-heavy.

Now, the size does limit the light output – this is nowhere near as powerful as their larger models. It also does not have variable light output as the larger models do. It just has an on/off switch. But for general lighting tasks, it works very well.

It comes with an internal lithium battery that is rated at 1200mAh and a charger for the battery. The battery is small and adds little weight to the device. I find that to be a big plus, since many of their larger models don’t come with a battery. On the downside, this will not run on AA batteries like their larger models do, so when the battery is dead you’ll have some downtime until it recharges (unless you buy a spare battery).

It has a hot shoe attachment for mounting on the camera. It can also be mounted on a tripod or light stand. The mount is plastic but reasonably well made. Note: although it has a hot shoe, it does not communicate with the camera in any way. You have to manually turn it on/off.

It does not come with filters, so the color temperature is limited to 6500K. That's a good point for general use, however.

This is a great choice for smaller cameras or for when you want to add some light but don’t want to deal with a larger unit. It’s easy to toss into a camera bag and carry along. The performance is excellent and the build quality is quite good given the price (especially since a battery and charger is included). Highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Bestlight Ultra-Bright LED 36 Camera / Video Light with Rechargeable Battery Pack and Charger for Canon, Nikon, Olympus, Pentax DSLR, Mini-DSLR and Camcorders

Her position is that care in the little things bodes well for the big things. Logitech demonstrates the same type of thoughtfulness with this device. First off, I was pleased and relieved to see that the the plastic clamshell encasing the mouse was easy to open. Nothing is more annoying than wrestling with difficult packaging. The mouse itself reflect the same degree of care. It looks chic. The outer design is entitled "Ink Gears". Upon close examination, you can see the little gears. However, it could just as easily be a pretty abstract design or even a floral pattern. In any event it is pleasingly chic.

The mouse itself is very comfortable. Although I am left handed, I usually scroll with my right hand. This mouse works well with both ands and scrolls smoothly and easily. The nano receiver can be stored in the mouse itself, helpful for on the road travel. The little receiver can also remain in the usb port of your computer. The battery is reputed to last a year and the on/off switch helps you conserve energy.

With its thoughtful design and ease of use, this mouse is ideal for everyday use.

text_fidelity_a:
ViewSonic 32 Inch 1080p Widescreen IPS Monitor with Ultra-Thin Bezels, Screen Split Capability HDMI and DisplayPort (VX3276-MHD) Caveat: for gaming, this is four stars. Its refresh rate is nothing noteworthy, and it lacks any kind of sync technology. My son and I swapped it in for each of his G-Sync monitors, and he said someone who'd never had G-Sync would probably like it a lot. Then, he took his own monitors back.

HOWEVER, when I took it to my husband's recording studio to test on Pro Tools, I almost had to fight him to get it back.

The QHD, blue screen filter, and other features make this perfect for anyone who is working long hours at anything that needs decent responsiveness and excellent resolution (film or photo editing, music production). The refresh rate is plenty good for Pro Tools, and the monitor is the best we've used so far at reducing fatigue.

Bottom Line: my son is keeping his G-Syncs, but my husband will be trying to wrestle me for the Viewsonic. I plan on keeping it in the home office, where he does some of his mixing and I watch streaming video. But he really wants to take it to his studio. And based on our field test of it there, that's where it really shines. So, we might be getting another one in the near future.
text_fidelity_b: ViewSonic 32 Inch 1080p Widescreen IPS Monitor with Ultra-Thin Bezels, Screen Split Capability HDMI and DisplayPort (VX3276-MHD)

text_fidelity_a:
Asus Nexus 7 2B32 7-Inch 32 GB Tablet, Black (2013 Model) 7 May 2014: Thanks to Google's omission of full USB OTG function, file transfers are frustrating & sometimes impossible. When I return home, I'm rooting it.

After 24 hours, I like it. It's a little different from my Galaxy Player 5 inch. The extra processor speed is nice. So is the combination of the light weight and larger screen. The GP5 was getting bogged down by software bloat. It fits nicely in my old K3 case. So far, so good.

...and it works with my Targus Bluetooth keyboard. Actually, it works better than it does with the GP5. The Samsung has some key-mapping problems, probably due to Gingerbread.

As to reading, I happened to be starting a novel the other day, and started it on the Nexus 7. I had no problem. I did keep the brightness on 'Auto', so the light level of the screen matched the ambient light. With the GP5, matching light levels was a little chancy, so I had a bit more eyestrain. (Of course the extra 2" of screen have no bearing on that, right?)

I did try the freebie 'La Luna' video that Google gives away. It watched fine on the 7" screen. The thing I really like is that there is a 7" screen in the weight of a past-technology 5" package. I owned a Nook color for 13 days, but took it back because of the weight and balance. It just wasn't comfortable to hold.

I haven't tried any significant music listening. I suspect I'll still prefer my Clip+ for that. The Nexus is a little large for that purpose. I also haven't tried the camera in any particular serious way. A selfie and a picture of my cat isn't much of a trial. Again, I'll probably use a purpose-made camera for real pictures. I also haven't explored portability yet. In the case, it's a bit bulky for easy transport, whereas the GP5 fits in my pocket next to my cell phone. I probably won't put the N7 in my pocket without a case. It's a little large and fragile seeming for that.

...As to the camera, it's OK, the image quality is fine, but a 7" tablet just isn't a good ergonomic platform for picture taking. This is the best from an afternoon at Mass Audubon's Ipswich River Wildlife Sanctuary.

Picture is available at:
MobileRead Forums > E-Book Readers > Android Devices>Nexus 7 2013 1st Impressions

...And I still prefer my Clip+ for music. I hand to hunt around the Android store for a decent player for my collection which includes WMAs as well as MP3s. Google does not play WMAs (cue prissy, superior sniff). I settled on Poweramp, not because it was perfect, but because it was the first one I came to that was good enough. I just want to listen to some music, people, not commit my soul to a single, ringing, crystalline-pure music player that rules them all. Sheesh.

Someday I may do a better review, too. All of the usual things about tablets are at worst adequate on the N7.

Oh, one piece of free advice, worth every penny you paid: Don't go hog wild buying really great accessories. Shop around. A $3 wire easel from a craft store will make a fine desk stand. I have one at work and one at home. A chopstick and a binder clip will do in a pinch. Also, there are good $10 EVA zip cases that will protect your N7 for transport. They don't have to be purpose built. My old K3 had a case that loosely fits the N7 (freebie!) and my KPW1 lives in a similar case. As to ear buds, the candy-colored $5 ones in the bin at the cash register at WalGreens are my favorite, and you never misplace them, because candy-colored.
text_fidelity_b: Asus Nexus 7 2B32 7-Inch 32 GB Tablet, Black (2013 Model)

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Basics Full Motion Articulating TV Wall Mount Bracket with Swivel and Tilt Features for 32-80 inch TVs and Flat Panels up to 130 Lbs, Black First of all, I'm looking at reviews and pictures of other peoples item and it seems they have a different item, and yet all the reviews are together. Let me start with the good...

PROS_ Inexpensive!

Cons_

THE INSTRUCTIONS: they are written in 6 different languages, and it jumps back and forth between them. It's not broken English, but very hard to follow. Some of them even have a sort of thumbnail of an entire page of text compressed into about 1.5." It is very bizarre. It took about 30 minutes of studying the pictures to figure out what the heck to do, because the manual certainly doesn't tell you. The box comes with sooo much extra hardware to account for different sizes and mounting situations, but the manual does not explain this well.

THE HARDWARE: It is super heavy duty and weighs nearly as much as my TV. My TV is super light weight and is probably 8 or 9 lbs. The bolts that screw into the stud could hold 100lbs I'm sure. Even pre-drilling pilot holes I had difficulty screwing them in with a drill they are so big. It takes so much torque that the screws stripped. I ended up using 1.5" wood screws. I used a stud and I don't like where the TV is mounted, so I am going to get molly bolts to screw it into the drywall where I would like to put it.

NOT STURDY: You mount a plate to the back of the TV, then you mount another piece of hardware to the wall. You then attach the TV to the hardware you just attached to the wall. It is wobbly. It also tilts anywhere from a perfectly neutral position to 20 degree or so angle down. This is in case you are mounting it very high and wish to tilt it down. The TV keeps flopping forward and tilting down. There is a bolt that keeps it in place and I tightened the heck out of it, and it just barely stays put.

NOT FLUSH: I have no other mounting systems to compare it to, but the TV sticks out about 2.5" from the wall. I was expecting it to be much closer.

So there you have it. I am not happy. Ultimately I have the mounted now and no real reason to return it because it's doing what I need it to. There are a lot of positive reviews, but they are I'm sure for a different product. Anyways I paid $15.95. You will most likely be happier with something you pay $25 for.

I included photos of the manual. You can see how the TV mounts, all the extra hardware, as well as a few pages of horrible manual- complete with the mini thumbnail pages.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Basics Full Motion Articulating TV Wall Mount Bracket with Swivel and Tilt Features for 32-80 inch TVs and Flat Panels up to 130 Lbs, Black

text_fidelity_a:
Coby Kyros 7-Inch Android 2.3 4 GB Internet Touchscreen Tablet - MID7012-4G (Black) I never owned a tablet or a smartphone so I suppose if I did my review might be different but I think this is a pretty neat little tablet and the price is pretty great too.

I've had it for a couple of days and downloaded the Amazon App store which has most of the apps anyone could need. I mean seriously how many apps does an average person really use? I have downloaded quite a few games for both myself and my kids, the Kindle app, I heart Radio app, and the US newspaper app. So far its holding all of it but I also ordered a microsdhc card for extra space to hold more apps and e-books. I have a regular Kindle that I've had for quite a few years and I am able to transfer most of the books onto this tablet also (I haven't tried downloading all of them since my son uses a few for school). It has where you can calibrate the stylus. Also if you longpress the stylus onto the wallpaper it will let you change the wallpaper in the background.

It does not come with a camera and flashplayer is not installed (but what I understand you can install a "lite" version of flashplayer which I have not done as of yet). The touchscreen is more geared toward using the stylus (which is included) which is a let down to some people. You can use your fingertip but it isn't as responsive as with the stylus IMO. It also comes with a sleeve (that has a place for your stylus) and earphones. There is a charger and a USB cable. There is another cable which I'm not sure exactly what its for (sorry). I haven't used the other cables just yet (except the charger of course). As for battery life it does seem like it runs down pretty quickly (perhaps 3-4 hours). Of course, that may change depending on the type of apps you have running. I know a lot of people worry about reading books from this rather than the Kindle type e-ink. I, personally, like reading at night before I go to sleep and with the Kindle I had to keep a lamp on just to see the page..(barely)...whereas this isn't like that (my eyes are much happier!) You can change the brightness of the screen if you are worried about the brightness bothering your eyes.

I have my email accessible to the Coby Kyros so I can check it throughout the day since my daughter takes off with my laptop quite often. I also downloaded the Dolphin mini browser which I like better than the browser sent with the Kyros. It comes with the GetJar app store which has quite a few apps but Amazon has more.

Of course, I cannot guarantee how well it will hold up because I've only had it for a couple of days but overall its a nice simple little tablet. I've seen the reviews of more expensive tablets and I don't want to spend $400 on a tablet that's rated two stars. I was willing to take the chance and so far I'm happy with my purchase. I rated it 4 stars because the speaker is kinda crappy...I haven't tried listening to the radio with earphones...hopefully it sounds better. And also I wish that it was easier to install flash (I've been looking on the internet but it seems like you have to be really a techie to do it...and I'm not!) It's not an Ipad (or Ipod) so you can't rate this tablet against a product like that (of course it's half the price of a Ipod touch).
text_fidelity_b: Coby Kyros 7-Inch Android 2.3 4 GB Internet Touchscreen Tablet - MID7012-4G (Black)

SABRENT USB 2.0 to DB25 IEEE 1284 Parallel Printer Cable Adapter [HEXNUT Connectors] (CB-1284) Although every new printer has a USB port, I have a few older, but still perfectly functioning printers that only have parallel inputs. I've been using those printers with PCs that have a parallel output port but, as those PCs get retired, it's getting harder to find a way to hook up the old printers. This solves that problem very well.

It's a simple cable. One end is a USB plug; the other is a DB25 female parallel port. IMPORTANT: you want to check your printer to make sure it can accept a DB25 female plug. Many printers only have a 36-pin Centronics input. If so, you need to get this one: [[ASIN:B00IDU0T1Y Sabrent USB to Parallel IEEE 1284 Printer Cable Adapter (CB-CN36)]]

The cable itself is decent. Thin, but the jacket feels more than sturdy enough for the job at hand. It's only 6 foot long which is OK for my needs but just barely. A longer version (10 or 12 foot) would be nice.

Works fine, and no complaints.
